Aerial Wildlife Survey Report 
Wildlife Management Unit 310 Aerial Ungulate Survey (2025) 
Background 
Aerial surveys are conducted periodically to obtain 
wildlife population estimates which assist biologists 
with species conservation management decisions.  
Wildlife Management Unit (WMU) 310 has historically 
been flown primary for large elk herds through a winter 
range survey, and not in a transect or block survey. 
This means that WMU scale population estimates 
have not been calculated from survey results before 
for moose, mule deer, or white-tailed deer, and this is 
a first for this WMU.  
The boundaries for the WMU are irregular shaped and 
generally follows landscape features such as 
watercourses, as well as anthropogenic features such 
as highways and forest reserve boundaries. The 
boundary of WMU 310 borders the Bow – Crow forest 
reserve to the west, secondary Highway 532 in the 
south, Highway 541 in the north, and Highway 2 to the 
east; however, only a small fraction (approximately 
150 km²) of WMU 310 has been surveyed for wintering 
elk in the past.  
The landscape of WMUs 310 is rolling and lightly 
forested, lying within the Foothills Fescue, Foothills 
Parkland, and Montane natural subregions (Natural 
Regions Committee 2006). The WMU is dominated by 
acreages and small farming operations, but also 
include numerous large farms and ranches. This 
region has a significant amount of ranching history 
(i.e., the Cowboy Trail, OH ranch, and Bar U Ranch 
National Historic Site). Industrial influences on the 
landscape include oil and gas extraction and forestry. 
Survey Method 
A transect survey was conducted in winter, with snow 
cover, to improve wildlife detectability. In the transect 
survey, all moose, mule deer, and white-tailed deer 
are counted and classified within a 400m buffer on 
either side of a transect line, and the total number for 
each species is used to determine a WMU scale 
population estimate. For elk, a minimum total count is 
recorded within the WMU. That is, all elk observed 
during the survey at any distance from the helicopter 
are recorded and classified. Based on the herd size 
and distribution of elk, many can be observed from 
more than one transect line for larger herds. The unit 
was last flown for elk in 2020 (Table 2). 
The transects were imposed over the landscape in 
east - west lines, in one-minute intervals across the 
entire 1065 km². East-West transects were chosen to 
capture the variability in topography for each line, 
since the eastern portion of the WMU is more open 
and agriculture based, and the western portion is more 
mountainous and treed. This reduces the variability 
between transects.  
Astar 350 FX2 helicopters were chosen for the survey 
with large side windows to improve visibility. Each 
helicopter had two observers in the back seat, one on 
each side, and a front observer on the left, with the 
pilot observing from the right. The navigator in the front 
carried a tablet using GPS real-time tracking system 
and the observers in the rear collected data of wildlife 
including, GPS location of group and line, species, 
classification (male, female, juveniles), cover (low, 
medium high), and behaviour (bedded, standing, 
moving). Classification was aided by high-definition 
images taken of groups. Elk were classified by sex 
(adult male, adult female, juvenile, or unclassified) 
based on presence or absence of antlers and on 
relative body size and shape of head. Bull elk with 
antlers were further classified as small, medium, or 
large based on standard antler classification criteria 
(ASRD 2010). Mule deer were classified as adult male 
(having antlers), adult female, or juvenile. Moose were 
classified into categories adult male (no vulva patch or 
antlers), adult female (vulva patch) and juvenile. 
White-tailed deer were not classified due to the lack of 
antlers remaining on most males. Other wildlife related 
observations during the survey were also recorded 
(e.g. sensitive wildlife features or species of interest). 
Results 
The survey took place on February 17th and 18th, 
2025. A total of 11.5 hours of survey time was required 
to complete all transects. 
Survey conditions were very good. Snow cover was 
100%; however, snow depth was relatively light. 
Temperatures ranged from - 29 to -25°C. Winds were 
low during the survey with the highest wind speeds 
estimated at 5 – 10 km/h. 
A total of 1135 white-tailed deer, 746 mule deer, and 
89 moose were observed within the 400m transect

(Table 1). Most moose and mule deer were observed 
west of highway 22, while white-tailed deer were 
equally observed both east and west of highway 22. 
The density of moose was lower than adjacent WMUs. 
This is likely because moose were only observed west 
of Highway 22, resulting in a lower calculated density 
for the entire WMU. West of highway 22, the 
population was healthy, though there were several 
observations of animals with tick-related hair loss. 
Mule deer and white-tailed deer were found to be at a 
higher density than WMU 312, which was flown in 
2024. Since no previous surveys within WMU 310 
included a population estimate for moose, mule deer 
or white-tailed deer, there is no comparison for 
previous years for these species within the WMU.  
Elk were observed primarily west of highway 22 (Table 
2) with a total of 838 being observed in the WMU. Bull
elk in the northern portions west of highway 22 were
classified to size. The number of juveniles per 100
cows was similar to previous surveys in WMU 310.
The percent bulls to cows was higher than observed in
the previous survey, likely due to the method used
Smaller groups of males can be observed with a 
transect method but would be missed when flying for 
large herds only as done previously. Of the 108 bull 
elk observed, 71 were classified: 44 were recorded as 
1-2 point (small), 24 were 3, 4 or 5 point (medium),
and 3 as 6 point or greater (large). The remaining were
unclassified. The elk population has steadily increased
since the last survey in 2020 and is currently at the
highest level observed in the unit (Figure 2). Several
groups on the northern and southern boundaries of
this unit share winter range between WMUs.
22 Sharp-tailed grouse, one golden eagle, 4 bald 
eagle, 2 foxes, and 38 coyotes were observed during 
the survey.
